about: Perpetua is followed by 'She' seven times and by one stray 'He' (the porter, unnamed); her gender must stay FEMALE.
title: The Cedar Trunk
author: Ada Pell

chapters.title: Departure
paragraphs: Perpetua rose before the household and lit the stove. She stirred the porridge until it shone.
Anselm came down the back stairs in his socks. He sat at the kitchen table and yawned.
Perpetua set a bowl in front of him. She watched him eat the first spoonful.
Perpetua spoke to the porter at the side door. He nodded and went to fetch the trunk.
The trunk was heavy and smelled of cedar. Perpetua lifted the lid and checked the linen.
She counted the sheets twice. Perpetua did not trust the porter's counting.
Anselm tied his boots by the stove. He was late, and he knew it.
Perpetua packed the last of the bread into a cloth. She tied the corners with a double knot.
At the gate Perpetua stopped and looked back at the house. She had lived there for eleven years.
Anselm shouldered the trunk. He carried it down the lane without complaint.
Perpetua walked behind him with the basket. She hummed a tune she had not hummed since childhood.
The carrier's wagon stood at the crossroads. Perpetua paid the driver and counted her change.
Anselm lifted the trunk into the wagon. He helped Perpetua up and climbed in after her.
Perpetua leaned against the cold boards. She closed her eyes and listened to the wheels.
The road ran east through flat country. Perpetua watched the hedges go by and said nothing.
Anselm slept with his hat over his face. Perpetua kept watch for both of them.
At the inn Perpetua asked for two beds. She paid in advance, as her mother had taught her.
In the district everyone knew Perpetua, and nobody had a bad word for Perpetua.
Years afterwards people still asked about Perpetua, though few could say why.
In the district everyone knew Anselm, and nobody had a bad word for Anselm.
Years afterwards people still asked about Anselm, though few could say why.
